title: Medicine show talk, Rena band, second-line bands and jitney dances
summary: Miller discusses whether the medicine was real, the Hadacol show, playing with Kid Rena in 1942, second-line parade bands, and how jitney or tag dances worked.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: About six or seven in the band you say? About six or seven in the band. About time, yeah. In other words, the band had a coffee in the show. Besides, you know, the performers and packing all the different medicine up and bringing around. Yeah. Yeah, about five, I know. I think about five, yeah. Was the medicine any good or was it just a racket? Some people say it was just soup. That's what I wonder. I've heard you. Some people say it was just soup. Or colored water and things like that sometimes. I think they take coke, they say, and put something in it a little bit. It gives us strength, that's all. Yeah. I guess it wouldn't hurt anybody anyway. Just like this outfit that little blonde brought out, you know. Oh, yeah. That had a call. Yeah. Well, it tasted something similar to had a call during that time. Yeah. It tasted something similar to had a call. He heard everybody buying had a call. Yeah. They had Sharky's band, I believe, traveled from them. Yeah. I think he still owed Sharky money. I remember seeing LeBlanc's, however the name is, LeBlanc or... LeBlanc, I see him. Yeah. In the union paper, you know. He defaulted on payments. That's right. He didn't even pay off the band. That's right. Supposed to be a big shot, too. I think a politician, wasn't it? I think a lot of the time. Yeah. Do you remember any of the other tent shows that they ever had here in town? Somebody told me once Ma Rainey used to travel in a tent show and would come here. Do you remember? Tim Rainey? Ma Rainey, a blues singer. No, I played music with Kid Rainey. Oh, Kid Rainey, yeah. I played music with him. Yeah. I played music with him and his brother, too. Oh, yeah, Joe. Joe is still around. I think he's a preacher or something. I played music with him when he was down by the Cadillac. He played down there for a long, many years. That's the only place I ever heard Kid Rainey, down at the Cadillac. I was down there. I bet I heard you maybe that night. Yeah. 1942, I believe it was. Yes. Now, who else was in the band besides Joe and Kid Rainey? Do you remember? I think Steve was playing clarinet. Who was this? Steve Angum. Steve Angum? I think Steve Angum. I think Steve Angum. Yeah. I think Steve Angum was playing clarinet there. You played piano? I still played the piano. Mm-hmm. Anything else about the parades when you were a boy? Did they have second line then, too, like they did? Oh, they had second line. Oh, they did. They had second line parade. They had second line parade. Now, the most band that door the crowd on second line parade, I know of, was a... Let me see the name of this band. Well, Pajo, he was a nice, he had a nice outfit. I remember Pajo, he was with his band. He was a Cliff Red band. Just lately I heard Sheep. Yeah. Pajo was in the Eureka too. Eureka band. But, uh... But, uh... And Pajo played down at the Budweiser too when I was a boy. That's where I met Pajo. Yeah. Yeah, I remember. He was down there with young. I remember... He was there a long time, I guess. Yeah. Did you ever play many of them? You said you played, I guess, most of those... What did they call them? Jitney dances? Jitney dances. Yeah. You buy tickets, so many tickets, your tickets run out. I remember the Budweiser. I played all those kind of dances. We called it the tag dance. Now, what hours did you have to work? The fellas talked like it was a pretty hard job, was it? You didn't... Oh, we didn't get no rest unless you just got off the stand. Yeah. In other words, you didn't get the dance, you didn't stop at all. And somebody take a solo, then you get off and maybe you take a walk some matter. When you come back, then they'll take a walk. Yeah. That's how we got our rest. But we played at the time. The only fella that didn't get no... He got rest too. The drummer. Somebody would go back there and get on their seat, whether they could play or not. Yeah, and beat it a little bit. Yeah, beat it a little bit during that time. Yeah. I don't know. Did it sound funny if the piano would stop out or somebody would take your plates? Well, you see, they didn't have these electric guitars during that time. They had upright basses then, you see. They used bass. Sometime that's the bass and the cytopop will be playing. Just the two of them like that. Yeah. This bass and the cytopop will be playing. Sometime the trumpet and the bass will be playing. How did it sound? Sometime the trumpet and the cytopop will be playing. Sometime the trumpet and the piano will be playing. The others will be gone. They wouldn't listen to the song, they would listen to the beat. They could still dance to it. They could still dance to it. They could still dance to it. Yeah. But the jitna dance wasn't the type of music like they're playing there now. In other words, you played a half a chord, maybe one chord and you're out, you're going to something else. You might play the Sheik of Arabi and Waltz time. They look again, you're playing something else. I asked a guy one night, I said, you don't play the Sheik of Arabi and Waltz time. I said, I played the star-ups from Waltz time. And I know they can't play. I played. When you be on the jitna dance, you play all types of music. We never did play no rumbles now. We didn't play no rumbles during the jitna dance.
